messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Carlos was fifty-three, he had been working as a counselor at a community mental health center for nearly two decades. He was good at his job—able to sit with clients in their worst moments and help them find a way through. On the day of the disaster, he was leading an afternoon anger management group. A client, a younger man whose case had been particularly difficult, had been escalating for weeks. That afternoon, the man stood up mid-session, picked up a metal chair from the circle, and hurled it at the wall beside Carlos. It missed his head by inches. Then the client overturned a table, sending papers and a coffee mug flying. In the chaos, a small electrical fire started in the corner where a lamp had been knocked over. The smell of burning wiring and melting plastic filled the room before the sprinklers came on. By the time the fire was out and the client was restrained, Carlos was standing in the soaked room, shaking, his ears ringing. He told himself it was over and that he was fine. But he wasn’t.

Over the months that followed, the burnt smell became a constant threat. It was not just actual smoke that set him off: a neighbor’s barbecue, a candle left too long, the scent of toast burning. Each time his nostrils caught that acrid note, his body reacted before his mind could catch up—heart hammering, palms slick, jaw clenched. He had come to believe that his body was his enemy, that it refused to accept that he was safe. Even sitting alone in his apartment, he would feel a wave of terror wash over him without any clear image attached; he would be flooded with the full emotional force of that afternoon—the helplessness, the suddenness—without being able to recall the chair flying or the flames. The memory felt distant when he did try to grasp it, like something that had happened to another person, someone he was watching in a film. But the feeling was all his.

He began to monitor his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance. Carlos was certain that if he let his mind wander anywhere near that day, he would unravel completely. So he became a kind of sentinel inside his own head, scanning for any drift, any stray image or smell, and slamming the door shut before it could take hold. At work, where his days were spent listening to other people’s stories of trauma, he found himself avoiding any client who talked about violence or fires, even though he had once been skilled at exactly those cases. He stopped attending the monthly staff meetings where colleagues sometimes debriefed difficult incidents, worried that someone would bring up that day. When a coworker asked how he was doing, he gave a curt “fine” and walked away.

His social life evaporated. He had always been someone who met friends for dinner or a drink on weekends, but now he found excuses—he was tired, he had paperwork, he had a cold. The truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of being around others. What if someone threw something in a disagreement? What if a restaurant kitchen had a smoky grill? He had to be especially careful, he told himself, because you never knew what could happen next. The world felt like a place where disaster was hiding around every corner, and only constant scanning could keep him safe. The isolation took its toll. His closest friend called twice, then stopped. Carlos spent most evenings alone in his apartment, eating microwaved meals, the television on low to fill the silence, but his attention was always half-cocked, listening for a siren, waiting for something to go wrong.

What finally brought him to therapy was a night when a car backfired outside his window. He dove to the floor, his hands over his head, and stayed there for nearly an hour, sobbing, unable to get up. The next morning he called a colleague he trusted and asked for a referral. Sitting in the intake office, he told the psychologist he was tired of being afraid all the time, but what he really wanted to know was whether he was going crazy. He said he couldn’t keep living like this, with his own mind and body turned against him, but he was terrified that if he let himself think about that day, even once, he would fall apart and never get put back together.
